reference_title: EM 1110-1-1905, Geotechnical Design of Shallow Foundations on Soils (USACE, 31 July 2025)

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: [p. 3] Shallow foundations are commonly used for support of light and moderately loaded structures. The typical design process for conventional shallow foundations and common foundation types are described in this chapter. Criteria is provided for evaluating the design loads with consideration to the design life, geotechnical limit states, factor of safety, reliability, intended structure function, and minimum code requirements.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-1, printed p. 3.

sections.title: Design process
sections.body: [p. 3] Like many design processes, shallow foundation design requires coordination with other design disciplines so that the geotechnical aspects can be integrated into the overall design. Where design requirements for shallow foundations cannot be achieved, deep foundations and ground improvement should be considered. Critical design aspects include:
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-2, printed p. 3.

sections.title: Uncertainty and risk
sections.body: [p. 3] Uncertainty and risk. Considerable uncertainty is inherent in geotechnical design. This uncertainty is primarily associated with load uncertainties, soil property uncertainty, testing method uncertainties, and the fact that the geotechnical engineer’s understanding of the subsurface are developed based on a very small sampling of the site. This uncertainty results in a range of possible design solutions, each with a different associated risk. Risk is further discussed in paragraph 2-3.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-2a, printed p. 3.

sections.title: Geotechnical investigations
sections.body: [p. 3] Geotechnical investigations. For foundation design, geotechnical investigations are performed so that subsurface conditions can be identified in the early stages of design. Insufficient geotechnical information could result in either an overly or non-conservative design, shifting responsibility to the contractor that could lead to differing site claims, and an increase in project scope. Some guidance is provided in Chapter 4. For more extensive site exploration details, reference EM 1110-1-1804.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-2b, printed p. 3.

sections.title: Geotechnical site assessment
sections.body: [p. 3] Geotechnical site assessment. Key objectives of a geotechnical site assessment for shallow foundation support are to establish baseline information, expected subsurface and hydrologic conditions, and evaluate engineering characteristics. A subsurface design model is an effective means of site assessment that is accomplished by summarizing and illustrating pertinent geological conditions and soil properties. The extent, complexity, and accuracy of the model is project specific and should consider quantity and quality of information available as well as the failure mode or limit state under consideration.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-2c, printed p. 3.

sections.title: Engineering evaluations
sections.body: [p. 3] Engineering evaluations. Foundations must be designed using the appropriate design loads and must satisfy requirements for ultimate and serviceability limit states presented in this manual. In addition, foundations must meet certain constructability and economic requirements. Once the shallow foundation support system is selected, it [p. 4] must be designed to provide the necessary support against expected and probable external loadings and should align with the site’s geologic and subsurface conditions.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-2d, printed pp. 3 to 4.

sections.title: Final design
sections.body: [p. 4] Final design. The structural engineer often prepares the foundation design based on structural requirements and the site-specific recommendations provided by the geotechnical engineer. Prior to final design, the geotechnical engineer should review the project information and contract documents to confirm their original design assumptions and recommendations were implemented as intended. If significant changes have occurred (such as changes in site grade, loading, structure location/layout), modifications to the foundation design or additional evaluation should be made so that the foundation can perform as intended.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-2e, printed p. 4.

sections.title: Construction observations and testing
sections.body: [p. 4] Construction observations and testing. Earthwork observations and testing are considered an extension of the geotechnical design and should be performed so that the field conditions can be reconciled with the design assumptions. The geotechnical engineer should coordinate with the foundation and earthwork field inspector and assist in resolving discrepancies encountered during construction that could conflict with the design intent. Additional guidance for earthwork observation and testing is provided in Chapter 12.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-2f, printed p. 4.

sections.title: Risk
sections.body: [p. 4] The term “risk,” as defined by USACE, is a measure of the probability and consequences of uncertain future events. Risk provides a framework for comparing project choices and informing decisions by a combined evaluation of hazard, performance, and consequences, considering their inherent uncertainties.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-3, printed p. 4.

sections.title: Risk assessment
sections.body: [p. 4] Risk assessment. Risk assessment can be performed during design or for existing structures. The USACE Risk Management Center (RMC) supports the development of methodology to support risk assessment for a variety of USACE missions as described in ER 10-1-55. The RMC has developed risk assessment procedures and has compiled practice guidelines for the purposes of dam and levee safety that can serve as a framework to support risk assessment of other project structure types. Contact the RMC for guidance if a risk analysis is planned.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-3a, printed p. 4.

sections.title: Risk assessment for new structures
sections.body: [p. 4] Risk assessment for new structures.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-3a(1), printed p. 4.

sections.title: Prescribed factors of safety in Allowable Stress Design (ASD) and Load and …
sections.body: [p. 4] Prescribed factors of safety in Allowable Stress Design (ASD) and Load and Resistance Factor Design (LRFD) should be used in designing foundations. These factors were established by various methods (such as statistical analysis, observations, experience) to better manage risk. The factors consider typical uncertainty of the loads, typical uncertainty of the resistance, and the typical consequences of a limit state being exceeded. For most structure designs, the prescribed procedures will result in acceptable risk.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-3a(1)(a), printed p. 4. The manual prints this subparagraph without a heading; the title is its opening words.

sections.title: For special cases, such as where a foundation failure would result in unusually …
sections.body: [p. 4] For special cases, such as where a foundation failure would result in unusually severe consequences such as loss of life or irreparable environmental damage, a risk analysis may help evaluate if a design using conventional factors is adequate to [p. 5] manage risk. Performing risk analysis does not allow reduction in standard design criteria. For scenarios in which the conventional design criteria are proposed to be reduced based on risk, guidance is provided in paragraph 1-6b.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-3a(1)(b), printed pp. 4 to 5. The manual prints this subparagraph without a heading; the title is its opening words.

sections.title: Risk assessment of existing structures
sections.body: [p. 5] Risk assessment of existing structures. Risk assessments may be performed to estimate the risk associated with an existing structure and to inform study decisions. Example project decisions that risk assessment can help inform include those associated with reduction in economic or safety risks.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-3a(2), printed p. 5.

sections.title: Geotechnical uncertainty
sections.body: [p. 5] Geotechnical uncertainty. Geotechnical uncertainty is the uncertainty of the estimation of the ground conditions due to lack of knowledge of ground conditions between and beyond exploration locations and due to limitations in the ability to measure and predict properties and behavior. Geotechnical uncertainty is adequately represented in most cases using an expected value and standard deviation terms. For example, the uncertainty of the effective friction angle of a sand could described as having expected value of 34 degrees and a standard deviation of 1 degree and an appropriate probability distribution model. Geotechnical uncertainty can be reduced by additional study such as exploration, laboratory testing, and performance monitoring (paragraph 2-6d). Geotechnical uncertainty is not the same as variability.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-3b, printed p. 5.

sections.title: Geotechnical variability
sections.body:
[p. 5] Geotechnical variability. Geotechnical variability is the actual range of geotechnical conditions that exist for a project and is sometimes called explained variation or natural variability. Variability is observed in material type, material spatial distribution, and material properties. The variability of the site cannot be reduced by additional study. The variability of the site is considered in foundation design by designing a foundation that has acceptable performance for the range of expected geotechnical conditions of a project, or by applying different foundation designs to different areas of the project.

[p. 6] Figure 2-1. Example of site variability vs uncertainty; red line denotes geotechnical material property for critical condition
figures: Figure 2-1: Example of site variability vs uncertainty; red line denotes geotechnical material property for critical condition
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-3c, printed pp. 5 to 6.

sections.title: Reliability analysis
sections.body: [p. 6] Reliability analysis. Reliability analysis consists of calculating a reliability index and probability of failure considering the loading and uncertainty of the geotechnical behavior. The reliability index is the probability that a limit state is not exceeded for a given load, and the probability of failure is the opposite. Duncan (2000) provides several geotechnical examples of reliability and probability of failure calculations. When performing reliability analysis, a common mistake is to confuse variability with uncertainty. If a weak or problematic ground condition is known to exist, the uncertainty of this critical condition should be used for evaluating reliability, not the variability of the conditions encountered at the site. Figure 2-1 illustrates this concept.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-3d, printed p. 6.

sections.title: Constructability and economic requirements
sections.body: [p. 6] Shallow foundations should be constructable using state of the practice means and methods. In general, the foundation design should be more conservative than the superstructure since poor performance impacts both the foundation and superstructure. In most instances, foundation repair costs are significant due to access constraints and impacts to building function which can require technically challenging solutions. In general, the appropriate type of foundation should represent a balance between performance, design, construction cost, and time. Of these, design cost is often the least significant. Where common construction methods or foundation design is excluded, a cost-benefit comparison with ground improvement and deep foundation support should be performed.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-4, printed p. 6.

sections.title: Shallow foundations
sections.body: [p. 7] Shallow foundations transfer and spread loads from the superstructure to the earth at shallow depth. They consist of isolated or combined spread footings, continuous (or strip) footings, ring foundations, and mats. For shallow foundations, the bearing area can, theoretically, be increased up to any practical size; however, there are some cases in which a shallow foundation should be analyzed as a mat, particularly if the footing is excessively long and wide, Refer to paragraph 8-2.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-5, printed p. 7.

sections.title: Footing depth
sections.body: [p. 7] Footing depth. The minimum vertical distance from the ground surface to the base of the footing is known as the depth of foundation (Df). This depth must be sufficient to meet strength and serviceability criteria, and the requirements of paragraph 2-8. Problematic ground conditions (such as expansive, frozen soils) and other functional requirements (such as adjacent structures) may require additional embedment. Guidance for problematic ground is provided in Chapter 10. Terzaghi 1943, defined a shallow foundation as having a width, B, equal to or greater than its depth, Df; however, subsequent research suggests Df/B could be as large as 2 to 4. For constructability purposes, maximum depths should generally not exceed about 6 to 8 ft.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-5a, printed p. 7.

sections.title: Isolated spread footing
sections.body: [p. 7] Isolated spread footing. An isolated footing provides support for an individual column, where the footing width (B) and length (L) have dimensions of B ≤ L ≤ 10B (Figure 2-2a). Isolated spread footings may be circular; however, they are generally approximately circular (octagonal) for easier constructability.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-5b, printed p. 7.

sections.title: Continuous spread footing
sections.body: [p. 7] Continuous spread footing. A continuous spread footing (also known as a wall or strip footing) has a length to width ratio of 10 or greater (L > 10B), (Figure 2-2b) and approximately meets the theoretical assumptions for plane strain conditions (see paragraph 6-6b) parallel to its long axis. Continuous footings typically support a single row of columns or a bearing wall. Continuous footings may be stepped to accommodate elevation changes in the structure or foundation bearing conditions if structural and code requirements are met.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-5c, printed p. 7.

sections.title: Combined footing
sections.body: [p. 7] Combined footing.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-5d, printed p. 7.

sections.title: General
sections.body: [p. 7] General. A combined footing consists of two or more columns that are supported by a rectangular (Figure 2-2c), trapezoidal, or T-shaped footing in lieu of two isolated spread footings. Combined footings are often used when the column spacing is very close and their individual footings or influence zones would overlap and can be used to resist large overturning moments in the longitudinal direction of the column row. For uniform distribution of pressure below a combined footing, the centroid of the footing should coincide with the resultant of the column loads.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-5d(1), printed p. 7.

sections.title: Strap footing
sections.body: [p. 7] Strap footing. A strap footing is a special type of combined footing that consists of two spread footings (proportioned with approximately equal bearing pressures) with a beam or strap connecting the foundations (Figure 2-2d). When two columns are far apart, a strap foundation can be used to transfer eccentric moment between two [p. 8] columns. For design, the strap beam should be rigid and unable to transfer load by not being in contact with the soil at its bottom contact surface. To reduce differential settlement, large differences in footing size should be avoided.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-5d(2), printed pp. 7 to 8.

sections.title: Ring foundation
sections.body:
[p. 8] Ring foundation. A ring foundation is essentially a continuous footing that is formed into a circle (Figure 2-3); and may incorporate an enlarged base. Ring foundations can be used to resist lateral loads and increase stability against overturning. The stress distribution under ring foundations is more complex than for a circular or rectangular foundation. Ring foundations are often used to support above ground storage tanks and silos and have no interior loading.

Figure 2-2. Types of shallow foundations

[p. 9] Figure 2-3. Example of ring foundation
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-5e, printed pp. 8 to 9.

sections.title: Mat foundations
sections.body: [p. 9] Mat foundations. Mats are large concrete slabs that supports column or line (such as wall or line of columns) loads in two directions and generally require negative moment reinforcing steel. Mats can be (1) thin (less than 1 ft thickness) supporting light structures, (2) ribbed or reinforced with cross beams, or (3) thick (greater than 1 ft thickness). Mats are generally considered when individual foundations occupy over 30 percent of the structure footprint area, where columns or walls would be placed so closely that overlap would occur, and where it is desired to reduce stresses in the soils. Mat foundations can be placed at the surface or extend to great depths (such as a fully compensated mat). Common mat types are shown in Figure 2-4.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-5f, printed p. 9.

sections.title: Ultimate limit state requirements
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-6, printed p. 9.

sections.title: Ultimate limit state
sections.body: [p. 9] Ultimate limit state. The ultimate limit state (ULS), also referred to as strength limit state, corresponds to a condition where the structure is judged to be unsafe. Geotechnical failure modes associated with this condition include: (1) bearing capacity, (2) sliding, (3) overturning moment and eccentricity, and (4) uplift.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-6a, printed p. 9.

sections.title: Allowable Stress Design
sections.body:
[p. 9] Allowable Stress Design. This manual incorporates ASD for working with design loads. For ASD, also known as Working Stress Design (WSD), a single, global factor of safety (FS) is used in foundation design to combine the uncertainties of loads acting on the foundation and the uncertainty of the resistance of the soil (or surcharge) to the load effects. Safety against failure is expressed, in the general form, as equation 2-1.

Load Effects, Q ≤ (Resistance of Soil, R)/(Global Factor of Safety, FS) [Eq. 2-1]

equations.description: Equation 2-1, introduced by: "Safety against failure is expressed, in the general form, as equation 2-1." (p. 9).
equations.formula: Load Effects, Q ≤ (Resistance of Soil, R)/(Global Factor of Safety, FS)

variables.FS: global factor of safety (minimum values in Table 2-1)

equations.notes: The general form of safety against failure in Allowable Stress Design (paragraph 2-6b); the print gives no list of symbols under it.

sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-6b, printed p. 9.

sections.title: Minimum factors of safety
sections.body:
[p. 9] Minimum factors of safety. Minimum factors of safety for shallow foundations are shown in Table 2-1 with exception to structures that are governed by EM 1110-2-2100 and EM 1110-2-2502.

[p. 10] Figure 2-4. Common type of mat foundations (a) flat plate, (b) plates with drop caps, (c) waffle mat, (d) mat with pedestals, (e) cellular mat, (f) ribbed mat

Table 2-1 Minimum factors of safety for ultimate limit state
ULS Failure Mode | Minimum Factor of Safety, FS
Bearing capacity | 3.0[1]
Sliding | 2.0[2]
Overturning moment and eccentricity | Note 3
Uplift | 1.5
Notes:
[1] Increases in allowable stress (for wind or seismic) must comply with the stipulated building code and UFC requirements (paragraph 2-8). Increases are not permitted where bearing soils are susceptible to shear strength loss (SSL), reference paragraph 9-10a. If a FS < 3.0 is used for design, additional settlement could occur due to partial yielding or plastic flow.
[2] Sliding (and passive resistance) are evaluated per paragraph 5-6. Factor of safety may be reduced to 1.1 for load combinations that include earthquake loads.
[3] For overturning stability, the factor of safety concept does not strictly apply when the resultant moves beyond the third point; eccentricity governs and is required to be within the inside middle-third of the footing.

sections.title: Limitations of Allowable Stress Design
sections.body: [p. 11] Limitations of Allowable Stress Design. For ASD, design parameters (such as material properties, strengths, loads) are assigned a single, deterministic value when the actual value is, in fact, uncertain. This means that the probability of failure (exceeding an ultimate limit state) cannot be directly estimated with this type of design analysis. To better support risk-informed decisions, risk and reliability analyses may be incorporated, reference paragraph 2-3.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-6b(2), printed p. 11.

sections.title: Performance monitoring
sections.body: [p. 11] Performance monitoring. Performance monitoring (such as settlement monitoring) may be used to better quantify the design assumptions. Performance data (visual, measured) should be assessed at appropriate stages to provide confirmation or denial of the characteristics assumed in design. If unacceptable performance is identified, the design should be modified until acceptable conditions exist.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-6b(3), printed p. 11.

sections.title: Serviceability limit state requirements
sections.body: [p. 11] The serviceability limit state (SLS) refers to a condition beyond which a structure becomes unfit for service and is judged to be no longer useful for its intended function. Serviceability requirements typically govern the design of shallow foundations and include total and differential foundation movements and durability. The selection of serviceability criteria should be coordinated with the structural engineer, architect, and owner, as appropriate, depending on the structural form and intended use. Guidance for allowable movements is provided in the following sections.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-7, printed p. 11.

sections.title: Allowable movements
sections.body: [p. 11] Allowable movements. Total and differential movements must be calculated for shallow foundations. Movements that negatively affect strength or serviceability of a structure are unacceptable; however, architectural considerations (such as appearance, cosmetic damage) may also influence acceptable tolerances. Allowable movements presented in this manual should be interpreted as “routine limits” and not as “rigid criteria.” Routine limits should not be applied to structures which are out of the ordinary or where loading conditions are markedly non-uniform. Allowable movements due to static loading conditions are presented in this section. Allowable movements due to earthquake loads are discussed in Chapter 9.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-7a, printed p. 11.

sections.title: Total settlement
sections.body: [p. 11] Total settlement. For most structures supported by spread foundations, total settlement should not exceed 2 inches; however, a typical specification for commercial buildings is 1 inch (Lambe and Whitman 1969). Mat-supported structures are commonly designed with total settlements not exceeding 2 to 4 inches; however, these limits may vary considerably depending on structure stiffness and serviceability requirements. For some structures (such as large flexible storage tanks on flexible bases), total settlements of 12 inches and greater can be tolerated; however, stricter tolerances are often stipulated due to serviceability requirements (such as piping connections, drainage). Total settlement should be calculated for a number of points across the footprint of the structure to establish the expected differential settlement pattern. Where differential settlements do not meet project requirements, total settlement should be reduced.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-7a(1), printed p. 11.

sections.title: Differential settlement
sections.body: [p. 12] Differential settlement.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-7a(2), printed p. 12.

sections.title: The physical basis for structure damage is maximum angular distortion because …
sections.body: [p. 12] The physical basis for structure damage is maximum angular distortion because maximum differential settlements may not necessarily be adjacent (may not result in maximum angular distortion). Both deflection ratio and angular distortion can give similar results as indicators for damage where hogging, sagging, and tilt are treated in a similar manner; however, angular distortion is generally considered more readily evaluated. During the design stage, angular distortion can be difficult to predict due to complex soil-structure interactions. Consequently, correlations with maximum total settlement and maximum differential settlement have been established for some common conditions (see paragraph 2-7a(2)(g)).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-7a(2)(a), printed p. 12. The manual prints this subparagraph without a heading; the title is its opening words.

sections.title: Control of differential settlement is generally accomplished by reducing total …
sections.body: [p. 12] Control of differential settlement is generally accomplished by reducing total settlement to tolerable levels. For example, a maximum total settlement of 1 inch would generally limit maximum differential settlements to less than 1/2 inch for most buildings. Where cut/fill activities are planned to achieve site grades, total and differential settlements should account for potential rebound due to excavation and settlement due to fills.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-7a(2)(b), printed p. 12. The manual prints this subparagraph without a heading; the title is its opening words.

sections.title: For estimating movements associated with expansive and collapsible soils …
sections.body: [p. 12] For estimating movements associated with expansive and collapsible soils, reference American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM) D4546 and ASTM D5333. Potential conditions that should be evaluated include:
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-7a(2)(c), printed p. 12. The manual prints this subparagraph without a heading; the title is its opening words.

sections.title: Soil heave and non-uniform wetting
sections.body: [p. 12] Soil heave and non-uniform wetting. Sum of the maximum settlement without soil wetting and maximum potential heave of the wetted soil.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-7a(2)(c)1, printed p. 12.

sections.title: Soil heave and uniform wetting
sections.body: [p. 12] Soil heave and uniform wetting. Difference between the maximum and minimum soil swell potential and depth of expansive soil subject to moisture changes and surcharge loads.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-7a(2)(c)2, printed p. 12.

sections.title: Soil collapse or shrinkage
sections.body: [p. 12] Soil collapse or shrinkage. Difference between the maximum and minimum total settlement with foundation and surcharge loading, assuming collapse (or shrinkage) does and does not occur.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-7a(2)(c)3, printed p. 12.

sections.title: Deflection ratio
sections.body:
[p. 12] Deflection ratio. The deflection ratio is a measure of differential movement (see Figure 2-5). The deflection ratio is defined by equation 2-2 as the maximum vertical deflection (Δ) divided by the horizontal length (L) over which the deflection occurs. The deflection ratio is considered a critical factor for unreinforced load-bearing walls which generally fail by sagging or hogging. In this respect, the length-to-height (L/H) ratio of the wall is significant; the higher the L/H ratio, the higher the limiting value of deflection ratio. Deflection ratio limits for unreinforced masonry walls are provided in Table 2-2. Larger deflection ratios than those shown in Table 2-2 can be accommodated if some of the settlement has occurred before installation of architectural finishes.

Deflection Ratio = Δ/L [Eq. 2-2]

[p. 13] where:
Δ = maximum vertical deflection between the tilt line of the building and two points on the imposed settlement curve (ft)
L = horizontal length between two points (Lsag or Lhog) on imposed settlement curve (ft)

Note. Actual deformations are perpendicular to the chord line Lsag or Lhog; however, the difference between the actual deflection and the calculated deflection (Δ) is inconsequential, and therefore, not considered.

sections.title: Angular distortion
sections.body:
[p. 14] Angular distortion. Angular distortion (β), also known as relative rotation, is a measure of differential movement and is defined by equation 2-3. Angular distortion does not distinguish between hogging and sagging, and it implies that damage is due to shear distortion within the structure, which may not necessarily be the case. Table 2-3 provides angular distortion limits for various structures. Larger angular distortions than those shown in Table 2-3 can be accommodated if some of the settlement has occurred before installation of architectural finishes. Empirical data suggests that typical buildings have architectural damage at β ≈ 1/300 and structural damage at β ≈ 1/150 (Skempton and MacDonald 1956).

β = δ/l [Eq. 2-3]

where:
β = angular distortion; also referred to as relative rotation (ft/ft)
δ = differential movement between two points (ft)
l = distance between two points, over which settlement has occurred (ft)

sections.title: Location of the maximum angular distortion
sections.body:
[p. 15] Location of the maximum angular distortion. For uniformly loaded, non-rigid foundations on cohesive soils, the maximum angular distortion typically occurs at the corner (Figure 2-6). For uniform loading on cohesionless soils and assuming a non-rigid foundation, the maximum angular distortion can occur anywhere on the foundation because the settlement profile is usually erratic (Figure 2-7). The location of maximum angular distortion does not necessarily correspond to the location of maximum settlement.

Figure 2-6. Regular settlement profile

Figure 2-7. Irregular settlement profile
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-7a(2)(f), printed p. 15.

sections.title: Correlations with maximum angular distortion
sections.body:
[p. 16] Correlations with maximum angular distortion. For steel or reinforced concrete frame buildings and load-bearing wall structures, Skempton and MacDonald (1956) and Grant et al. (1974) reported correlations with maximum angular distortion (equations 2-4 and 2-7). A crude correlation was reported for the footings bearing on clay and a fair correlation was reported for the footings bearing on sand. In general, the maximum angular distortion for a given maximum settlement is smaller for clays than for sands or fills. For mat foundations, correlations with maximum angular distortion are more complex due to the influence of mat rigidity and should be considered directly by soil-structure interaction, refer to Chapter 8.

Isolated foundations on clay*

ρmax = 1,200 × βmax [Eq. 2-4]

Δmax = 550 × βmax [Eq. 2-5]

Isolated foundations on sand or fill*

ρmax = 650 × βmax [Eq. 2-6]

Δmax = 350 × βmax [Eq. 2-7]

where:
ρmax = maximum total settlement (in) *not applicable where deep-seated clay contributes to settlement
Δmax = maximum differential settlement (ft/ft)
βmax = maximum angular distortion; also referred to as relative rotation (ft/ft)

sections.title: Tilt
sections.body:
[p. 16] Tilt. The rotation of the entire superstructure or a well-defined portion of the structure resulting from differential movement is referred to as tilt (ω) and is defined by equation 2-6. Rigid body tilt can be difficult to evaluate since it depends on the deformation capacity of the structure, which is influenced by the type of foundation. Limits for tolerable tilt of a building are usually related to serviceability rather than collapse. For low-rise buildings, the maximum acceptable tilt should not exceed 1/400. Variations in tilt limits for some other structures are listed in Table 2-4.

ω = SV/L [Eq. 2-8]

where:
ω = tilt (ratio)
SV = differential movement (edge to edge) of entire structure or defined portion (in)
L = span of entire structure or well-defined portion (in)

Stacking of goods | 1/100

sections.title: Lateral movement and uplift
sections.body: [p. 17] Lateral movement and uplift. A serviceability limit state check is not required for shallow foundations. It is intended that shallow foundations have very little lateral and uplift movement. Guidance provided in paragraphs 5-6 and 5-7 is intended to conform to this condition. For retaining and floodwall structures, tolerable movements are described in EM 1110-2-2502.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-7a(3), printed p. 17.

sections.title: Heave
sections.body: [p. 17] Heave. Soil heave may occur from expansive soil activity “swell” or due to excavation-induced stress relief or “rebound.” For expansive soils, maximum allowable swell potential due to expansive soils (even without foundation surcharge), should not exceed 1 inch for foundations placed above where volume change occurs or above expansive soils (O’Neill and Ghazzaly 1977). Differential movements should not exceed those based on foundation settlement. Typically, ground improvement or other mitigation efforts (such as drainage improvements) are necessary for suitable shallow foundation support. Where soil rebound may occur, foundation total and differential settlements should meet the criteria presented in this chapter.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-7a(4), printed p. 17.

sections.title: Collapse and shrinkage
sections.body: [p. 17] Collapse and shrinkage. Maximum allowable settlement potential (under full surcharge and foundation loading) due to wetting-induced soil collapse or shrinkage of expansive soils should meet requirements for total and differential settlement. Typically, ground improvement or other mitigation efforts (such as drainage improvements) are necessary for suitable shallow foundation support.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-7a(5), printed p. 17.

sections.title: Durability-related serviceability limit
sections.body: [p. 17] Durability-related serviceability limit. The integrity of foundations embedded in soil can be adversely affected by chemical and biological processes that can cause deterioration. A durability-related limit state is intended to ensure foundations can resist these processes and provide adequate performance over the design life. The durability limit state is often associated with corrosion of steel reinforcement or degradation of concrete due to environmental (such as freezing/thawing, water) or chemical (such as sulfates, chlorides) exposure.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-7b, printed p. 17.

sections.title: Steel reinforcement
sections.body: [p. 18] Steel reinforcement. Corrosion resistance of reinforcing steel is primarily provided by concrete cover over the reinforcing steel that reduces contact with the surrounding soil and water. Minimum clear cover requirements for reinforcing steel and alternative methods of protecting steel reinforcement are provided in American Concrete Institute (ACI) 318 and should be verified prior to concrete placement, see also EM 1110-2-2104 for hydraulic concrete structures.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-7b(1), printed p. 18.

sections.title: Concrete exposure
sections.body: [p. 18] Concrete exposure.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-7b(2), printed p. 18.

sections.title: Shallow foundations are normally constructed of reinforced concrete, which can …
sections.body: [p. 18] Shallow foundations are normally constructed of reinforced concrete, which can remain intact for many years in most soils. In certain environments, where concrete is exposed to freezing/thawing conditions or chemical exposure (such as sulfates, chlorides, salt) degradation can occur. Exposure categories and classes, and requirements for concrete by exposure class, are provided in ACI 318 for some common conditions. In some cases, the exposure categories can be influenced by design functions or construction activities and may not be solely a function of pre-construction site subsurface conditions.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-7b(2)(a), printed p. 18. The manual prints this subparagraph without a heading; the title is its opening words.

sections.title: The exposure category and class should be designated by the structural engineer …
sections.body: [p. 18] The exposure category and class should be designated by the structural engineer based on the site-specific subsurface conditions reported by the geotechnical engineer and the design conditions. The geotechnical engineer should be familiar with the requirements of ACI 318. For especially severe exposure (such as acid exposure), a corrosion engineer should be engaged.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-7b(2)(b), printed p. 18. The manual prints this subparagraph without a heading; the title is its opening words.

sections.title: Unified Facilities Criteria and Building Code requirements
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-8, printed p. 18.

sections.title: General
sections.body: [p. 18] General. United Facilities Criteria, UFC 1-200-1 is the overarching document for buildings and facilities used by the Department of Defense (DoD). UFC 1-200-1 directs use of the International Building Code® (IBC), the International Existing Building Code® (IEBC), Core UFC, other UFC as applicable to the building, facility, structure, or system, and Facility Criteria (FC) as they pertain to the applicable DoD component. USACE has a wide range of building types in the Civil Works Directorate Building Portfolio, and some building types (such as pumping stations, powerhouses) require an enhanced level of analysis or design due to associated risk. Reference ER 1110-2-8161 and ER 1110-2-1806.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-8a, printed p. 18.

sections.title: Presumptive load-bearing values
sections.body: [p. 18] Presumptive load-bearing values. Presumptive values should not be used in final design of shallow foundations; however, they may be used for preliminary evaluation of shallow foundation feasibility. Presumptive values do not account for footing configuration, eccentricity, or load/footing inclination and could vary greatly from actual field conditions.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-8b, printed p. 18.

sections.title: Design life
sections.body: [p. 19] The design life for USACE military projects is typically 25 to 50 years, and for civil works projects is typically 50 to 100 years. In some cases, major projects can remain in use indefinitely, see ER 1110-2-8159.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-9, printed p. 19.

sections.title: Foundation design loads
sections.body: [p. 19] For ASD, foundation loads (often referred to as unfactored loads) are provided by the structural engineer for evaluation of the ultimate limit state (strength design). Building codes provide very little commentary on serviceability loads because code requirements are intended to provide a reasonable level of safety and property protection and are not intended for economic viability of structures.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-10, printed p. 19.

sections.title: Load application
sections.body: [p. 19] Load application. Various types of loads (such as static, dynamic) can be applied to a shallow foundation. Foundation design methods in this manual assume static load conditions unless due to earthquake. For seismic design, failure zones are mostly based on an assumed static failure surface (pseudo-static) and various parameters are used to characterize these loads. Guidance for shallow foundations subjected to seismic loads is provided in Chapter 9.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-10a, printed p. 19.

sections.title: Design loads for ultimate limit state
sections.body: [p. 19] Design loads for ultimate limit state. For military structures, criteria for design loads used for evaluating ultimate limit states are provided in UFC 3-301-01. For new civil works buildings, requirements are outlined in ER 1110-2-8161. For civil works hydraulic structures (such as dams, spillways, locks, pumping stations, floodwalls), guidance is provided in EM 1110-2-2100 and EM 1110-2-2502.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-10b, printed p. 19.

sections.title: Loads causing settlement
sections.body: [p. 19] Loads causing settlement.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-10c, printed p. 19.

sections.title: For settlement evaluations, service loads are used
sections.body: [p. 19] For settlement evaluations, service loads are used. Typically, the dead load plus some portion of live load is recommended. There is a significant difference between live loads estimated from building codes for evaluating the strength limit state (ultimate limit state) and those necessary for evaluating the serviceability limit state. Live loads used in building codes for evaluating the strength limit state represent the maximum live loads that could occur during the life of the structure and are intentionally higher than have been measured during arbitrary live load surveys (these live loads are higher than would be expected to be sustained for long periods).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-10c(1), printed p. 19. The manual prints this subparagraph without a heading; the title is its opening words.

sections.title: For settlement evaluations, live loads should not be reduced by more than 50 …
sections.body: [p. 19] For settlement evaluations, live loads should not be reduced by more than 50 percent. The amount of live load reduction should be based on knowledge of the intended use of the structure (such as duration of live load, time-settlement behavior).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 2 (Design and Performance Requirements), paragraph 2-10c(2), printed p. 19. The manual prints this subparagraph without a heading; the title is its opening words.

sections.title: Typical building foundation loads
sections.body:
[p. 19] Typical building foundation loads. Typical line and column loads for buildings are described in Table 2-5 and are based on a survey of some engineering firms. An understanding of typical loads is useful as a general reference during design or for preliminary studies; however, should not be used in final design unless verified by the structural engineer.

[p. 20] Table 2-5 Some typical loads on building foundations
Structure | Line Load (kips/ft) | Column Load (kips)
Apartments | 1 to 2 | 60
Individual housing | 1 to 2 | < 1
Warehouses | 2 to 4 | 100 to 200
Retail spaces and two-story buildings | 2 to 4 | 100 to 150
Multi-story buildings (< 4 stories) | 4 to 10 | 200 to 300
Schools and administrative buildings | 2 to 6 | 100 to 150
Industrial facilities | varies | 100 to 200
Notes:
1. Tall multi-story structures can have column loads exceeding 2,000 kips.
2. Column spacings are often 20 to 25 ft or more.
3. The average pressure applied per story of a building often varies from 0.2 to 0.4 tsf.
